title: Specialisation & division of labour
examples: What is the main benefit of specialisation for a country?
Can specialisation ever be a drawback?
How does the division of labour increase output?

explain.say: Today we will learn about specialisation and division of labour. This means doing one specific job. It helps us make things faster and better.
The first benefit is increased efficiency. When people only do one task, they become very quick at it. Think about building a car, one person does only the wheels.

items: Step 1: One person builds whole car (Slow)
Step 2: Many people build one part (Fast)

explain.say: Another benefit is higher quality goods. Because workers repeat the same task often, they become experts. This means the final product is usually very good.
However, there are drawbacks to consider too. If one person does everything, they might get bored or tired. This can sometimes lower overall morale.

items: Workers might feel disconnected from the whole product.

explain.say: A real-life example is a large bakery. Instead of everyone making bread, some people mix the dough, others bake, and others decorate. This makes many loaves quickly.
A common mistake is thinking that more people always means better results. Remember that the way the work is organised matters most. Specialisation needs coordination to work well.

draw.text: Mistake: Assuming more people is always best

faq.q: Does specialisation only happen in factories?
faq.a: No, it happens everywhere we work. Even in a school, some people teach maths while others teach history. It is about dividing tasks.
asks: Where can I see division of labour?
Is specialisation only for big businesses?

faq.q: If I only do one job, will I learn other skills?
faq.a: It is harder to learn many different skills if you only do one thing. This is a drawback because you miss out on variety.
asks: Can I become too narrow in my skills?

faq.q: Is increased efficiency the only benefit?
faq.a: No, higher quality and faster production are also benefits. It helps the whole economy grow stronger and richer.
asks: What else is good about specialisation?

faq.q: What is the opposite of specialisation?
faq.a: The opposite is generalisation, where one person does many different tasks. This is called being a generalist worker.
asks: What is the word for doing many jobs?

faq.q: Does specialisation mean people lose control?
faq.a: Sometimes, yes. Workers might feel like they are just small parts of a huge machine. This can affect their job satisfaction.

facts: Specialisation means focusing on one specific task or area.
The division of labour increases the total output of goods.
A drawback can be job monotony, which leads to boredom.
Experts in one area can produce goods of very high quality.

quiz.say: A large printing press has separate workers for setting type and running the machine. This is an example of:
quiz.why: This shows different tasks being separated for speed.

wrong.0: Trade involves exchanging goods between different places.
wrong.1: This is a negative outcome, not the name of the process.
wrong.3: This means doing all the tasks yourself, which is slower.

quiz.say: If a worker only ever polishes one type of shoe, the main benefit they gain is:
quiz.why: Repetition makes the worker an expert, improving the finish.

wrong.2: Specialisation always aims to increase speed.
wrong.3: While true, 'higher quality' is the main economic benefit.

quiz.say: A drawback of extreme specialisation is:
quiz.why: Doing the same simple task repeatedly can be mentally draining.

wrong.1: Specialisation usually leads to higher overall wages.
wrong.2: The problem is with the task itself, not the planning.
wrong.3: The drawback is often a lack of variety, not too much freedom.
